items.title: A Pure Physical Ship Antifouling Structural System Based on Geometric Space Constraints:Mechanism Hypothesis and Engineering Pre-research Scheme
items.abstract: Ship underwater barnacle biofouling continuously increases hull frictional resistance and raises fuel consumption of ocean-going cargo ships, while traditional copper-containing antifouling coatings face increasingly strict international marine environmental protection regulations. Existing chemical coatings, flexible thorn films and microcavity self-locking structures have engineering defects such as attachment failure, sharp rise in navigation resistance, adhesive peeling and sediment silting. This paper proposes a modular external steel structure system with streamline longitudinal high-low conical ribs and embedded micro serrations. Narrow groove cavities and point-line contact block the lateral expansion of barnacle larva base, and segmented streamline water barriers prevent organisms from forming long strip calcified shells along the heading direction. A supporting anchor directional spray system solves the problem of sediment silting and slot blockage in stagnant water ports.The complete engineering design is established in this paper: steel skeleton is externally installed by intermittent spot welding without modifying the ship base metal; homogeneous carbon steel strip triple sealing structure completely avoids seawater galvanic corrosion and gap water seepage; a multi-component navigation resistance splitting model is constructed, and two-stage drag reduction optimization plans are set to strictly control the additional frictional resistance within 10%. Four core scientific hypotheses verifiable by sea trials and CFD simulation are put forward, and a digital quantitative observation index system and full-life cycle inventory cost model are established. At present, all structural design, risk prevention and control and verification paths are fully closed. Subsequent fluid simulation, 12-month real sea panel exposure test and component fatigue corrosion test only need to be carried out. After data verification, real ship segmented pilot transformation can be carried out. This purely physical non-chemical antifouling technology is expected to become a new technical route for green drag reduction and marine antifouling on existing ocean-going vessels.

items.title: Design and fabrication of microstructured PDMS surfaces for antifouling and drag reduction
items.abstract: Abstract Marine biofouling on ship hulls substantially increases hydrodynamic drag and operational costs. This study selects the barnacle, a sessile crustacean with strong adhesion ability, and develops polydimethylsiloxane films patterned with micro-cylinders to achieve dual-functional antifouling and drag reduction based on the barnacle larvae dimensions and hydrophobic principle. Bioassays with barnacle cyprid larvae demonstrated that the microstructured surfaces significantly inhibited settlement, achieving an antifouling rate of 59%. Rotational drag tests further revealed a maximum drag reduction of 7.2% at 100 rpm. To elucidate the physical mechanisms, computational fluid dynamics simulations using the volume of fluid model were conducted. The numerical results verified the stability of the entrapped gas-liquid interface within the microstructures and revealed a substantial reduction in near-wall turbulence intensity and shear stress, quantitatively validating the slip-effect mechanism. These combined experimental and numerical results demonstrate the potential of engineered microstructured surfaces for marine antifouling and drag reduction applications.

items.title: Simple drag prediction strategies for an Autonomous Underwater Vehicle’s hull shape
items.abstract: The range of an AUV is dictated by its finite energy source and minimising the energy consumption is required to maximise its endurance. One option to extend the endurance is by obtaining the optimum hydrodynamic hull shape with balancing the trade-off between computational cost and fluid dynamic fidelity. An AUV hull form has been optimised to obtain low resistance hull. Hydrodynamic optimisation of hull form has been carried out by employing five parametric geometry models with a streamlined constraint. Three Genetic Algorithm optimisation procedures are applied by three simple drag predictions which are based on the potential flow method. items.title: Bio-Derived Dual-Temperature Antifouling Coating Enabled by Oyster-Shell Valorization
items.abstract: Oyster-shell waste represents an abundant biogenic calcium carbonate resource with potential for conversion into functional marine coatings. This study investigates a waterborne acrylic coating incorporating oyster-shell powder thermally treated at 600 °C and AZO@SiO2 core–shell nanoparticles. During a 12-month natural-seawater deployment at Anping Harbor, the three coated panels showed markedly lower visible macrofouling than the uncoated controls, although localized deposits were visible, whereas uncoated controls exhibited substantially greater visible surface coverage. Adjacent uncoated structures also showed spatial differences in fouling coverage, although these field observations do not establish the underlying biological mechanisms. Under laboratory illumination of 100 W m−2, the coated surface reached an apparent temperature of 42.1 ± 1.8 °C at 90 s, compared with 31.2 ± 0.8 °C for the uncoated control, corresponding to an apparent temperature difference of +10.9 °C. Preliminary gas chromatography–mass spectrometry (GC-MS) measurements revealed time-dependent and spatially varying analytical signals tentatively associated with low-molecular-weight amines. The proposed volatile-amine-mediated deterrence and photothermal antifouling mechanisms remain hypotheses requiring controlled biological validation. In preliminary 28-day leaching tests, Cu, Zn, Sn, and Fe concentrations were below the corresponding instrumental detection limits under the tested conditions. The estimated material and basic processing cost was approximately US$4.50 m−2, subject to further economic validation. These findings demonstrate the potential of oyster-shell waste valorization for developing functional marine coating systems while identifying the analytical, ecological, and durability investigations required before broader practical deployment.

items.title: Assessing the vulnerability of Antarctic marine ecosystems to invasive non-native species
items.abstract: Invasive non-native species are a major threat to global biodiversity. For at least 15 million years coastal Antarctica has been poorly connected to nearby temperate ecosystems due to physical and physiological barriers. Yet, Antarctica is experiencing significant environmental change and becoming increasingly exposed to ship-borne human activity that crosses the physical barriers. These factors may facilitate the establishment of non-native marine species. This doctoral research adds insight into the risk of non-native marine species being transported to Antarctica via ships’ hulls and internal seawater systems, with particular focus on pathways of introduction and species found within those pathways. To begin my research, I assessed the current knowledge of non-native marine species in the Antarctic region: the physical and physiological factors that resist establishment of non-native marine species; changes to resistance under climate change; the role of legislation in limiting marine introductions; and the effect of increasing human activity on vectors and pathways of introduction. Evidence of non-native marine species was limited: up to 2019 just four marine non-native and one cryptogenic species that were likely introduced anthropogenically had been reported free-living in Antarctica or in the sub-Antarctica islands, but no established populations have been reported. An additional six species had been observed in pathways to Antarctica that are potentially at risk of becoming invasive. I estimated there may be approximately 180 vessels and 500+ voyages in Antarctic waters annually. However, these estimates are necessarily speculative because relevant data are not recorded comprehensively. In response to the scarcity of data on ship movements into the Southern Ocean, I obtained data on ship activity in the Southern Ocean from 2014-2018 inclusive and developed a ship traffic network for Antarctic-going vessels. I analysed the ship movements and conducted a spatially-explicit assessment of introduction risk for non-native marine species in all Antarctic waters. I found that vessels connect Antarctica via an extensive network of ship activity to all global regions, and especially South Atlantic and European ports. items.title: Aerodynamic forces on high speed multi-hulled marine vehicles
items.abstract:
The need for high-speed high-payload craft has led to a considerable interest in
vehicles capable of bridging the gap between conventional ships and aircraft. One
such concept uses the forward motion of the craft to create aerodynamic forces on
a wing-like structure, and hence, alleviate the overall drag by reducing the wetted
area.
This research focuses on the use of suitably shaped multihull geometries to
achieve e cient aerodynamic lift for high-speed sea vessels. The problem is  rst
studied in two dimensions using a simpli ed analytical approach and CFD modeling.
The work is then extended into three dimensions and a  nal aerodynamic
model is produced for a complete hull form, including the e ects of hydrodynamic
surfaces above the water. The aerodynamic analysis demonstrates that signi cant
e ciency can be achieved through careful shaping of the side hull and cross deck,
with lift-to-drag ratios of nearly 50 for a complete aerodynamic hull con guration.
Further analysis is carried out using a hybrid vehicle stability model to determine
the e ect of such aerodynamic alleviation on a theoretical planing hull
vessel. Comparisons are made using the Savitsky planing model, and from this it
is found that the resistance can be almost halved for a  fty metre, three hundred
tonne vehicle with aerodynamic alleviation traveling at 70 knots.
A comparative study is made for the hybrid vehicle with regards to size, speed
and weight, whilst attempting to match the proportion of aerodynamic lift with
speed to a theoretical optimum. From this the likely con gurations for future
development are identi ed
